summary: Defines TLS handshake extensions for exchanging authorization data, such as attribute certificates or SAML assertions, once both sides say they support it. The data goes in a supplemental data handshake message. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5878 defines a way for TLS clients and servers to exchange authorization information during the handshake. The peers first negotiate supported formats, then send authorization data in supplemental data messages.

questions: how to send saml assertion in tls
what is supplemental data in tls
subtitle: TLS handshake extensions for exchanging authorization information.

tldr.problem: Some TLS environments need authorization information exchanged before protected application data is sent.
tldr.mechanism: Client and server hello extensions negotiate supported authorization formats, then supplemental data messages carry the information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5878 is Experimental, updates RFC 5246, and was updated by RFCs 8447 and 8996.

today: RFC 5878 is Experimental and updates RFC 5246; it was updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996. It was published for examination, experimental implementation, and evaluation.

sections.title: Authorization Before Application Data
sections.content:
TLS authorization extensions let a client and server exchange authorization information before protected application data flows. The same authorization information may be useful to more than one application using the TLS session.

The formats are extensible. The RFC defines X.509 attribute certificates and SAML assertions, and permits other formats. It also cautions that authorization tied to one application may be better carried inside that application's TLS-protected data.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS can carry information about what a peer is allowed to do, in addition to identifying the peer. This is most useful when several applications can use the same authorization information.

sections.title: Negotiating Authorization Formats
sections.content:
The client_authz extension indicates formats the client can send to the server. The server_authz extension indicates formats the client can receive from the server. The server replies with the formats it accepts or can provide, removing formats it does not support; it omits an extension if no listed format is acceptable.

Authorization data is sent only for a format both sides negotiated. A client should include the extensions when requesting session resumption, because the server may reject resumption and continue with a full handshake. A resumed session must use the same authorization information as the original session.
sections.plainLanguage: The client lists the authorization formats it supports, and the server indicates which ones it can use. If they share no format, that authorization data is not exchanged.

sections.title: Authorization Data and Supplemental Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines four formats: an X.509 attribute certificate, a SAML assertion, and a URL-and-hash form for each. The URL forms are provided because the full authorization objects can be large. Implementations using these forms must support HTTP URLs and verify that the downloaded object matches its hash; SHA-1 and SHA-256 must be supported.

The authorization information is carried in a SupplementalData handshake message using the authz_data type. A client should send only the authorizations the server is expected to need. The RFC does not support a handshake exchange where the server returns new authorization information in response to the client's data.
sections.plainLanguage: Authorization information can be sent directly or fetched from a URL and checked against a hash. The handshake carries the data in a supplemental message after the peers agree on its format.

sections.title: Errors and Assigned Values
sections.content:
The RFC reuses TLS alerts associated with certificate processing to report authorization failures. All alerts used for authorization processing are fatal. For example, an authorization that is corrupt or not trusted can stop the handshake, and an unavailable authorization URL must result in denied access.

IANA assigns client_authz as extension type 7, server_authz as type 8, and authz_data as supplemental data type 16386. The document also creates a registry for authorization formats, with the X.509, SAML, and URL forms as its first four entries.
sections.plainLanguage: If authorization data is invalid, unavailable, or insufficient, TLS stops the connection. The RFC also assigns identifiers so peers can recognize the extensions and data formats.

sections.title: Protecting Sensitive Authorization Data
sections.content:
Authorization data in the ordinary handshake is sent before the client is authenticated, and the supplemental message is not encrypted at that point. A bearer SAML assertion could be captured and replayed. The server must also restrict access to only applications and features for which authorization was confirmed.

For sensitive data, the RFC describes a double handshake: first establish protected communication without authorization extensions, then perform another handshake with the authorization data inside that protection. This also ensures both parties are authenticated before they provide authorization information.
sections.plainLanguage: Authorization information can be exposed if it is sent in the first handshake. A second handshake inside an already protected session can limit who can read that information.
